::: {#exm-logistic-wald}

#### How little six patients tell us

For the fit of @exm-logistic-regression, `vcov` returns $\inv{\tp{X} \hat W X}$.

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
# standard errors: square roots of the diagonal of (X'WX)^-1
wf_se <- sqrt(diag(vcov(wf_fit)))
wf_slope <- coef(wf_fit)[["wf_x"]]
# 95% Wald interval for the slope
wf_ci <- wf_slope + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * wf_se[["wf_x"]]
# the groups sit two units apart, so the group odds ratio is exp(2 * slope)
wf_group_or <- exp(2 * wf_ci)
wf_summary <- c(
  slope = wf_slope, se = wf_se[["wf_x"]], lower = wf_ci[1], upper = wf_ci[2]
)
round(wf_summary, 3)
```

The interval for $\coef{1}$ is $(`r round(wf_ci[1], 2)`, `r round(wf_ci[2], 2)`)$.
The odds of recovery in the treatment group are $4$ times those in the control group,
with interval $(`r round(wf_group_or[1], 2)`, `r round(wf_group_or[2], 1)`)$.
The interval runs from a strong harm to a large benefit,
consistent with the non-significant test of @exm-deviance-drop:
six observations are far too few for this large-sample approximation to be reliable,
and the interval says so.

:::
